lines.text: One of the oldest towns on Earth, a city holy to three faiths, empires, exile and a modern state at war. This is the story of Israel and its land.
About twenty million years ago a rift began to open here. In it lies the Dead Sea, whose shore is the lowest dry land on Earth.
In the Jordan valley, people settled at Jericho about eleven thousand years ago, building a stone tower and walls.
In the hills above, Jerusalem took root, a city that would become holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims alike.
In the Bible's telling, King David made Jerusalem the capital of Israel.
After the exile in Babylon, the Temple in Jerusalem was rebuilt, later expanded by Herod, and destroyed by Rome in the year seventy.
Meanwhile scribes were copying sacred texts. Found near the Dead Sea in 1947, the scrolls hold the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible.
Herod's fortress on the rock of Masada would become the last stand of Jewish rebels against Rome, until the year seventy-three.
Under the Roman emperor Constantine, a church rose over the place Christians believe Jesus was buried, drawing pilgrims ever since.
Many centuries later, after Byzantines, caliphs, crusaders and Ottomans, the journalist Theodor Herzl founded political Zionism.
David Ben-Gurion, born in Poland, would lead the Zionist movement and become Israel's first prime minister.
Golda Meir, born in Kyiv and raised in America, moved to Palestine and would one day become prime minister.
In 1917 Britain declared its support for a Jewish national home in Palestine, without harming the rights of others there. Rival claims soon clashed.
Yitzhak Rabin, born in Jerusalem in 1922, would become a general, then prime minister, and sign a peace accord.
In 1948, as the British Mandate ended, Israel was declared a Jewish state. Its borders remain disputed to this day.
On the fourteenth of May, David Ben-Gurion read out the declaration of independence.
Neighbouring Arab states joined the fighting that followed, and about seven hundred thousand Palestinians left or were driven from their homes.
In 1949 Benjamin Netanyahu was born. He would become Israel's longest-serving prime minister.
That year Israel also formed Mossad, its foreign intelligence agency.
In 1953 Yad Vashem was founded in Jerusalem to remember the victims of the Holocaust and record their names.
In 1961 Adolf Eichmann, captured by Mossad in Argentina, was tried in Jerusalem, and survivors' stories reached the world.
In June 1967, in six days of war with Egypt, Jordan and Syria, Israel took Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan.
In 1973 Egypt and Syria struck by surprise on Yom Kippur. Golda Meir led Israel through the war, and an oil crisis followed.
In 1976 Israeli commandos flew to Entebbe in Uganda to rescue hostages.
In 1978, at Camp David, Sadat and Begin reached the agreements that brought the first peace between Israel and an Arab state.
In 1993 Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed the Oslo Accords, and Rabin shared the Nobel Peace Prize.
Two years later an Israeli extremist shot Rabin dead at a peace rally.
Meanwhile firms like Mobileye, which makes driver-assistance chips, made Israel known as a start-up nation.
In October 2023 war came to Gaza, and it would bring great loss of life.
It began on the seventh of October, when Hamas-led fighters killed about twelve hundred people in Israel and took two hundred and fifty-one hostages.
In June 2025 Israel and the United States struck Iran's nuclear sites, and Iran fired missiles back, in a war of twelve days.
A small land with a long memory, whose story is still bound up with war and the hope of peace.
